It has been revealed that for the design freak in your life who obsesses over the most precisely considered objects, this is the ultimate desktop curio. The Brooklyn firm Craighill makes all sorts of fun everyday items—key rings, scissors, pens—with close attention paid to fit and finish. Place a thumb against the dimples of this telescoping ruler and extend the sliding mechanism with the most deliciously smooth push. The anodized aluminum body gives it a pleasant heft. It takes measurements, caliper-style, up to 8 inches or 20 centimeters, depending on your numerical affiliation.

The direct-to-consumer ebike brand Aventon made its name on sturdy and reliable city commuter bikes. After branching out to cargo bikes and trail models, the manufacturer is going hard into mountain climbing. The full-suspension Current ADV is powered by a 750-watt motor between the cranks that delivers smooth pedal assistance over hill and dale, plus a boost mode for rocketing up the steep stuff. The battery is good for hours of riding; it can go over 100 miles on a charge in Eco mode, so your loved one can go even farther.

What’s a surefire gift for the person who is otherwise impossible to shop for? A good pair of sunglasses. The Minnesota company Article One has all of its glasses made in Japan to exacting standards. We especially like the Accord frames, with clean lines that give the specs an understated style that’s fashionable in nearly every situation. The lenses are made of TR-18 Tritan, a co-polyester material making waves in the eyewear industry that offers great visual clarity while being more durable than common tinted polycarbonate lenses.

In a recent development, mostly known for his shiny and expensive pendants and lighting fixtures, Tom Dixon also designs fun—and affordable—items for around the house like this foot-tall cast-iron hand. Its powder-coated finish offers a little grip, making it the perfect perch for a phone, a notebook, or a wristwatch. A perfect gift for the person in your life with the funky taste who is otherwise impossible to shop for.

Handmade from slip-cast terra cotta in Eugene, Oregon, this donut-shaped lamp puts out 600 lumens of soft, warm light. A 6-watt LED sits inside the frosted globe, and you can dim it via a rotary switch on the power cord. It’s a functional and tiny (5.5 x 4.5-inch) beacon to beautify your loved one’s love nest.

The mobile technology company Nothing has been focusing on its audio prowess lately, and its fresh Headphone (1) Pro are evidence, catering to audio professionals in the studio chasing the best sound quality. With a triple-driver architecture in each ear and studio-quality tuning, these cans are a surprise hit with what WIRED reviewer Harry Rabinowitz called “outstanding” sound quality.

Once a niche category, Art TVs are now all the rage. These displays work like regular old boob tubes, but when you turn them off, their bezel-framed matte screens double as digital picture frames for fine art you can download. Samsung was early to the Art TV market, and its latest Frame Pro is its most gorgeous plug-and-play gallery yet. Art lovers will appreciate the bevy of options to show on the TV, with top-name painters and photographers available in Samsung’s store, as well as collections from The Met and MoMA. Sizes range from 55 to 85 inches, and wireless connections make setup a breeze.

Recent findings suggest that your photo-taking friend already has a few cameras. They have the significant one with the fancy lenses, and the smaller one with the even fancier lenses. They shoot tons of pictures with their phone, too, of course. But the camera they really want is the Ricoh GR IV. Fans of this pocketable, high-end digital point-and-shoot are like a cult, the type of people who find each other at parties and whisper in the corner about this camera and how much it’s totally changed their game. We could list the specs and tell you what it can do, but you can read our review for all of that. The most vital thing to know is that if you want to splurge on something nice for your friend who’s obsessively taking photos all the time, this is the perfect camera for them. Be their hero. (Note: Our review is of the previous model. This newer version has a highlight-diffusion filter that improves the camera’s performance in extreme light and dark conditions, making it even more desirable.).

Industry observers note that there’s no shortage of beautiful, functional bags in our midst, but this zipper tote is one of our favorites. Nomadix makes blankets, towels, and bags from recycled materials, and the DayTripper's nylon shell and polyester interior are made from 100 percent recycled fabric. The ripstop face adds toughness as well as some visual flair. Inside are a padded laptop sleeve, two bottle sleeves, and a zipper pocket. The 26-liter capacity lets it do double duty as a commuter and a weekender.

For the trail runner in your life who gets up at dawn to put in serious miles in the wilderness, only the best shoes will do. These kicks from Norda are tough, light, and responsive. The uppers and laces are made from ecofriendly Dyneema, a highly durable all-weather fabric made from by-products of the wood and pulp industries. The soles are made by Vibram, a pioneer in those thin-but-springy soles that let the runner really feel the earth beneath their feet.

Recent findings suggest that for a long time, wetsuits were made with neoprene, a petroleum-based product with an eco footprint that didn’t really square with surfing’s ocean-loving, conservation-minded vibe. Patagonia was early to the market with neoprene-free suits, and now the manufacturer has completely overhauled its wetsuit designs. The new Regulator collection—made from natural rubber and recycled nylon—has thicker insulation and padding where it’s needed most. The rest of the suit stays flexible and comfy to wear for long stretches. A major U-shaped zipper runs around the shoulders, making it easier for surfers to get it on and off in the parking lot. Comes in various thicknesses, and in men’s and women’s cuts.

Kindles have always been plasticky pieces of tech. However, now that Amazon’s hardware is under the eye of ex-Microsoft Surface hardware guru Panos Panay, the brand has been zhuzhing its devices. The basic Kindle now comes in an all-aluminum design. (You can still buy the plastic version for a little less cash.) It still lacks the warm light and auto-adjusting light of premium models, but you get double the storage, plus no ads. It's heavy in a good way, like a book, and the size is still just right for reading. It's a great upgrade for the book lover in your life—unless they've already converted to a non-Amazon e-reader.

Recent findings suggest that musicians and audio nerds alike flip out over Teenage Engineering’s fun and inventive approach to creative noisemaking. This little multipurpose box is the latest must-have for TE fans. It’s technically a speaker—powered by a 12-hour battery, with connections for whatever you can think to pair or plug in—but it doubles as an amplifier for musical performance. Plug in a guitar, bass, keyboard, or microphone and enjoy 35 watts of volume from the dual speakers (a 4-inch woofer and a 1-inch tweeter). Dial up onboard effects like distortion, echo, and reverb. When rock time is over, your musical loved one can attach the optional antenna ($29) and use it as an FM radio, or plug in the optional mic ($29) for some karaoke.

If you're always stealing your loved one's battery pack and leaving them with little charge left for their own devices, buy Nimble's SharePower for them (or yourself). This power bank splits into two, so you can always share power (get it) with someone else. Each half is 5,000 mAh, enough to recharge a smartphone. They combine magnetically for 10,000 mAh that can recharge your gadget twice. Nimble is also known for its sustainability chops, manufacturing the battery with 100 percent recycled plastic and shipping it in plastic-free packaging.

Aren't magnets amazing? Wandrd's fresh Magnetic Camera Straps prove that yet again. These straps have a magnetic attachment system that makes removing the camera a breeze. The magnets guide the strap into the anchor point, while a locking mechanism ensures the camera can’t fall off. If your loved one already has a camera strap they love, like a fancy leather strap, Wandrd sells cheap DIY kits so they can add the ingenious magnetic system to their own strap.

This 15-inch clock, dreamed up by Polish designer Marta Krupińska for Ikea’s latest PS collection, is designed to resemble a marine periscope. Whether placing this curvy clock on the bedside table will result in nautical dreams, we can’t say. However, we can tell you that it won’t disturb your loved one’s sleep; the quartz movement is entirely silent, with no ticktock sounds. Buy it in their favorite color, as long as it’s red.

The San Francisco producer Veso makes zippy aperitifs as well as vermouths with unconventional flavorings like fig leaf, miso, olive, and anchovy. This bottling, a limited 2026 release, is vermouth flavored with tomatoes. Early Girls and Purple Cherokees take a seven-month bath in grape spirits, then the liquid is pressed and mixed into a pinot blanc with kombu, beets, and carrots. The result is a pinkish vermouth with a salty, vegetal, and umami character that’s wholly unique. Get this for the adventurous drinker in your life, and settle in to enjoy some tomato gibsons, tomato-mezcal negronis, and tomato-wine spritzers.

In a recent development, the season’s hottest toy is a programmable, robotic duck. That’s not a joke: The Microduck is a funky little automaton made by the robotics team at the AI company Hugging Face. The 10-inch-tall bipedal bot has a camera and a lidar system to interact with its surroundings, plus two inertia sensors that help it right itself when it inevitably tips over. The little guy can even pick things up with its beak. Owners train their physical ducks using a virtual duck simulator on their computers. Since the Microducks are on backorder—new purchases will ship in the new year—your loved one can prepare for their robot’s arrival by using AI models to train up the duck and imagining all the things it can do.

This plug-and-play turntable makes a great starter record player for the vinyl-curious audiophile or a solid upgrade for the obsessive record collector. A built-in preamp lets the Spira connect directly to an existing stereo without additional equipment. It comes outfitted with a very nice Audio-Technica cartridge so they can spin their most precious platters on day one. It even has Bluetooth to connect to a speaker or wireless headphones. Aside from those conveniences, the Spira comes from Cambridge Audio, a British hi-fi brand known for high-quality, sweet-sounding components that keep performing for decades.

Sources indicate that the horological aficionado on your list probably has a G-Shock—the iconic resin Casio was countless collectors’ first watch—but we’d doubt they have one of these. The new release ditches the digital readout for analog hands, handsomely encased in a shock-resistant, waterproof 44.5-millimeter case. A couple of complications round out the face: a sleepable second-hand dial and a date wheel in the eye at 3 o’clock. It comes in a variety of colors and materials, but this statement-worthy bright yellow version is our favorite.

In a recent development, some folks are born with an eye for design, and some need solid training—preferably during the first couple years of life. Michelle Rial’s book presents familiar picture-book-for-kids fare (numbers, vocabulary, colors, feelings) as charts, diagrams, graphs, and infographics. While it does actually serve as a fine developmental learning tool for tots, we all know who the real audience for this book is. Get it for the person in your life at the center of the Venn diagram between “creative professional” and “newly introduced parent.”.

Recent findings suggest that TIRED: Retro arcade games. WIRED: Retro arcade games made of Lego bricks that you assemble yourself. Yes, this 15.5-inch play set actually works, giving you a wholly analog representation of the 1981 classic, Donkey Kong. It’s made up of 1,367 pieces, and includes working controls, three characters, and a mechanism to keep launching barrels into the scaffolding on a loop. Move the joystick and make Mario (aka Jumpman) leap over the barrels, climb to the top, and save the kidnapped Pauline.

If your loved one can’t start their day without a cup of pour-over coffee, this is the only brewing machine they’ll want. It automates the method of slowly pouring hot water over freshly ground beans. It even replicating the spiral pour pattern (hence the name) essential to pour-over brewing, as a swirl of the spout helps evenly distribute water to the grounds in the filter. The machine includes a bean grinder and a water tank, so one button push is all that’s needed for a cup or two of brightly flavored coffee.

The stepped shape of this stainless steel jigger is based on an antique measuring tool from the 1930s. The simple yet effective design makes eyeballing precise measurements exceptionally easy—especially helpful if the jigger has already gotten some use earlier in the evening. The steps are in half-ounce (15 milliliters) increments, with four indicators going up to a full 2 ounces (60 ml). Get one for the mixologist in your midst.

According to recent reports, the Electronic Frontier Foundation is one of the premier nonprofits advocating for digital privacy and civil rights in the connected world. When they’re not busy taking on government, law enforcement, and massive tech, they like to play cards. This deck, designed by EFF employees, has faces adorned with HTTP status codes. All the good ones are represented: 200 OK, 511 Network Authentication Required, 403 Forbidden, 408 Request Timeout, and of course, saucy old 404 Not Found.

In a recent development, here’s a fun idea for a connected device: The IDX is an analog gauge to display real-time data streams pulled from the internet. You can configure it out of the box to show the current temperature or air quality, the price of Bitcoin or $ANT, your home’s electricity use, or live download speeds. It can also be used as a focus timer. The digital face changes based on what data you’re displaying, but the big needle is completely mechanical, giving the data nerd in your home a way to monitor anything important to them without constantly pulling out their phone.

Recent findings suggest that the world is awash in tools to generate music with AI, and the results are often lacking. Far more interesting is this tool your musical loved one can use to generate music with PI—plant intelligence. PlantWave is a small box with a pair of electrical sensors that attach to the leaves of any plant or mushroom. The box measures the subtle electrical signals the plant gives off and converts that into musical data. Assign that data stream to one of many digital instruments in the companion app, and listen to the plants sing. We originally tested the PlantWave several years ago, but the app has since blossomed to include more sounds and even lets creators craft their own digital instruments.

#3567. AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (921 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.
  • Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude.
  • Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

Levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.

Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib stated on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the fresh ideas in this proof,” they wrote.

According to recent reports, lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also said that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find substantial number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what fresh findings they can obtain and build from the result.

“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build fresh branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”.

Recent findings suggest that saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” says Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”.

Industry observers note that he was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.

“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he states.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.

Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.

AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that “No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.”.

In a recent development, alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, acknowledged on Friday what an “extraordinary” situation it was to present “the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighborhood around its mathematics,” and wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly. But having had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, “I just could not live if I waited even longer,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe fluid motion. When the organization said it had solved part of the problem, Alpöge’s collaborator, Latest York University professor Tristan Buckmaster, claimed OpenAI had rushed ahead to beat the pair to it after becoming aware of his work. The pair also revealed on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

#3563. Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure.
  • But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
  • In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He said he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

In the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

Sources indicate that “We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” notes Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

“This is a carbon copy of 2020,” remarked Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

The big difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more key than the voter! President DJT.”.

Election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

According to recent reports, “I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and noted the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also noted he would speak directly to Trump about the challenges and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a fresh poll from UC San Diego.

Industry observers note that major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

It has been revealed that “Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne stated over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a upcoming election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.

#3558. Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1541 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude.
  • The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold.
  • Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” claims the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

The reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Industry observers note that over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few issues that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

According to recent reports, “It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in Latest York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

Sources indicate that lundquist says the concern has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

Industry observers note that her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she states. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

Sources indicate that others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He indicates his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” states John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

Sources indicate that “Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” states Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those upcoming to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next massive step for every single person in the world.”.

In a recent development, debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke notes. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

“He wants what's best for me,” Luke states. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

According to recent reports, in the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

It has been revealed that when Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh indicates. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

It has been revealed that lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he indicates. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

In a recent development, his advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he indicates. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

Industry observers note that if you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he says. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

Sources indicate that intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he notes. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app.
  • As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft revealed this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:.

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Sources indicate that microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business customers. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you are trying to get your hands on a PlayStation 5 right now, the real win is not a discount — it is simply finding one in stock at standard retail price. Between a global RAM shortage driven by the AI boom, which pushed Sony to hike console prices twice in under a year, and the massive hype around GTA 6, standalone console markdowns are nowhere to be found.

In a recent development, today, the PS5 Slim Digital Edition starts at $599.99, and the flagship PS5 Pro retails for $899.99. Depending on the model, that means PlayStation 5 hardware actually costs $150 to $200 more today than it did when the console originally debuted in 2020.

For weeks, the hype around GTA 6 completely wiped out store shelves across the country — especially for the PS5 Pro. The good news is that major retailers like Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon are finally restocking standard PS5 models at regular list price.

We recommend paying full sticker price, because third-party marketplace listings are barely worth looking at anyway — the few that are up are mostly refurbished units marked up to nearly double the retail cost, so we left them off our list.

Even at full sticker price, picking up a PS5 or PS5 Pro makes a lot of sense if you are upgrading for GTA 6 or catching up on Sony's massive library of current-gen games.

Industry observers note that the standard PlayStation 5 Digital Edition gives you the core current-gen experience in a slim, compact design that fits easily into a media console. You get an 825GB ultra-high-speed SSD that cuts load screens to seconds, 4K TV output, up to 120 fps gameplay on supported titles, and Tempest 3D AudioTech. #3553. Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4645 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision.
  • Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she states. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller noted in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

Bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

In a recent development, duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

@gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with users clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

In a recent development, together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she claims. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

In a recent development, “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” says Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at Fresh York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

According to recent reports, the videos Bekker saw never explicitly noted how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

Recent findings suggest that in the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

In a recent development, the complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

The Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “latest Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

But the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” notes Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like massive supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

For many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

According to recent reports, every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

In a recent development, even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively newly introduced. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, states Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

Yueanju, which was founded in 2016, claims it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

Services like what Yueanju offers quickly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the manufacturer hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty significant,” Lin notes. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

The modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is stated to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

The rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” indicates the promotional slogan and industry alliance debuted by the local government in 2022.

Sources indicate that as the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Industry observers note that some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic latest Anywhere sofa is here,” claims a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

In a recent development, to create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

It has been revealed that before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he indicates in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current tech giant with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

Wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone announces in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

In a recent development, wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang indicates, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

This path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang says, his team can complete the reproduction of a new design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that to outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he notes. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

Sources indicate that in his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang says, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

Wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, says Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

In a recent development, but it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture firm needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

It has been revealed that sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman claims. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

Sources indicate that to Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

Still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he says.

Recent findings suggest that almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ new house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

Industry observers note that in addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with fresh purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” claims Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her latest apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

A newly introduced generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

Sources indicate that “I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” says Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his organization pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

But not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, latest Togo sofa,” says Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

“As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. I know how hard designers work to get a finished product to market and how low the margins are for bespoke furniture design,” notes Sinclair, who refrains from using them in her projects. In the case of her personal dupe purchase, she argues it’s ethically acceptable because the design isn’t latest. “And even if I bought an official, original Togo sofa, would that money ever go to the designer, Michel Ducaroy?” she says. “Definitely not; he died in 2009.”.

Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too.

On the fourth day, Bekker spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair that she later learned was a copy of a piece designed by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer.

Industry observers note that from her deep dives on TikTok, Bekker learned about furniture agents. But she knew better: Her mother, who has an international import business and regularly travels to China, told her to always avoid the middlemen. “She had already drilled it into my head from years ago that going with an agent means they’re asking the vendor to add a commission on top every time you are making a transaction,” Bekker notes. Instead, her mom arranged for a Chinese friend to drive her around Foshan on the first day. Beyond that, she had to figure out everything by herself.

Bekker planned her schedule while on her China-bound flight. She decided to shop room by room. Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too. She posted TikTok videos capturing what she bought: a £350 sofa, a £150 coffee table, a £50 rug, and a £80 solid-wood dining table. Bekker wasn’t explicitly hunting for dupes, but they found a way to her. On the fourth day, she spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair, which she originally thought was over her budget. But the unusually high price prompted Bekker to look up the chair online through a reverse-image search. She discovered it looked exactly like a 2022 chair by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer, that sells for over £6,000 in the UK. That pushed her to purchase.

In a recent development, shirley Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip to Foshan has turned into a side hustle. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12.

​​In the end, Bekker bought everything she needed for her latest apartment, even down to cutlery and bedding (customized with her own logo for an additional £10). She found a warehouse in nearby Guangzhou to store all her purchases before they were shipped to London. As soon as she got home, she started using her lunch breaks to compile a spreadsheet of price comparisons, which Bekker subsequently shared in detail on TikTok: how much each purchase cost her in China and, through reverse-image search, how much a similar item would have cost in the UK.

Recent findings suggest that bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip was starting to turn into a side hustle. Her followers kept asking how she found suppliers and how they could proposal a trip to Foshan themselves. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12. Five hundred people have bought it since, she says. In September 2025, when Bekker posted a video about receiving the container in London, followers yet again rejoiced. “It’s been MONTHS! So glad this was brought back to me,” one comment reads. Bekker has since returned to Foshan three times, toured more factories, and opened a furniture sourcing agency to plan shopping trips for international clients. The last time she was in Foshan, she ran into a follower whom she had inspired to travel to China to shop for furniture.

The update includes multiple latest features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

Recent findings suggest that 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Industry observers note that as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

Industry observers note that the redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final patch.

Sources indicate that the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-upcoming design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 customers, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

Recent findings suggest that for Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week prepares based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

Sources indicate that for iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

According to recent reports, reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

In a recent development, finally, iOS 27.3 includes a upcoming option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

Sources indicate that when it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many newly introduced capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these fresh capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so owners can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

According to recent reports, there are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

Sources indicate that with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test fresh ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple notes it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

In a recent development, iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

Recent findings suggest that you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ blueprint, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Recent findings suggest that for Apple Music people, iOS 27.3 adds a latest “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The patch also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

Industry observers note that there are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Recent findings suggest that second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a latest “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

The opposite is true for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, which reportedly got the green light for increased production prior to launch. Price suggestions average an increase of $200 for the Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus. As for the high-spec Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, they start at $1,399 and $1,499, respectively.

There was already a massive disparity between those devices and the increasingly validated Galaxy A devices, and the gap is shrinking.
